title: The Seam Where ROS 2 Plugs In: Writing a Node Against an Interface and Testing It Without ROS

questions.question: Why write a component against an interface instead of directly against rclcpp?
options: Written against rclcpp it can be tested only where ROS 2 is installed and processes can talk; against an interface it runs in a test in microseconds and a ROS 2 adapter is one class
An interface is faster to call than rclcpp, since it avoids the middleware for every message
rclcpp cannot run more than one node in a process, and an interface can
Written against an interface the component needs no tests, because the adapter is tested by ROS 2
questions.explanation: The component asks its node for publishers, subscriptions, timers and the time, and nothing else. In a test those come from an in-process node, and on a robot from one class over rclcpp.

questions.question: Two nodes run the same component, one in /robot1 and one in /robot2. A number is sent to robot1's input. Who handles it?
options: Both: they run the same component, so they share its topics
Only robot 2, which was created later and took over the name
Only robot 1: it handled 2 messages and robot 2 handled 0, because relative names resolve in each node's namespace
Neither: a relative name is not delivered until it is remapped
questions.explanation: The component writes in, and each node resolves that in its own namespace: /robot1/in and /robot2/in are different topics.

questions.question: A node is destroyed while its subscription is still registered on the bus. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the bus drops subscriptions whose node has gone
The next message calls into a component that no longer exists
The bus stops delivering that topic to every subscriber
The message is queued until a node with that name is created again
questions.explanation: The subscription is a function that captures the component. If it outlives the node, the bus calls a function whose object is gone.

questions.question: What did the test measure after a node with a subscription and a timer was destroyed?
options: Nodes alive 1, subscribers to its topic 0, and 0 calls into it in the 5 s and 10 messages after
Nodes alive 0, subscribers to its topic 1, and 10 calls into it afterwards
Nodes alive 1, subscribers to its topic 1, and 2 calls into it afterwards
Nodes alive 2, subscribers to its topic 0, and 1 call into it, from its timer
questions.explanation: On destruction the node took back every subscription and timer and removed itself from the world. Before that it had been called twice; after, never.

questions.question: Why is a node's timer armed when it is created and not at its first poll?
options: So that timers fire in the order the nodes were created
Because a timer armed at its first poll would fire twice in its first period
So that the timer's first firing is at time zero
A timer made at 0 and first polled at 0.6 s would have lost the whole of its first period
questions.explanation: The period starts when the timer is made. Over 3.5 s the status timer fired 3 times, at 1, 2 and 3 s.

questions.question: What does this lesson not claim about ROS 2?
options: That names resolve by the rules of 17-11, which were only checked for one namespace
That an adapter satisfies the interface: the sketch is not built or tested by this repository's CI, which has no ROS 2 lane, and has to be checked wherever ROS 2 is installed
That the component's tests pass, which needs ROS 2 to confirm
That a node cleans up after itself, which only rclcpp can show
questions.explanation: The lesson checks that the seam has the right shape. Whether an rclcpp class really implements it has to be checked on a machine with ROS 2.
